   2 │ 
   3 │ ## What happens now
   4 │ 
   5 │ When I give my subcommands a shared object through the pass decorator, every subcommand refuses to run unless some outer command built that object first.    7 │ ## What should happen
   8 │ 
   9 │ I want to tell the pass decorator to build the object for me when it is missing. Then a subcommand that is run on its own still works, using a fresh empty object, and an outer command can still set values on the same object for its subcommands to use.
  10 │ 
  11 │ ## About this project
  12 │ 
  13 │ This project is Click, a Python library for building command line programs. You describe your commands with decorators, and Click takes care of parsing options, printing help, and passing values into your functions.
  14 │ 
  15 │ ## Problem this solves
  16 │ 
  17 │ Without a way to have the object created on demand, every command in a group has to repeat the same setup code, and the subcommands are unusable unless the user happens to call the top level command in the right order. That makes help text misleading and forces me to keep the setup in sync across every command.
  18 │ 
  19 │ ## What changed
  20 │ 
  21 │ Two things users can do now that they could not before. First, the running command's context can be asked for an object of a given type and will hand back a newly created empty one when nothing of that type has been stored yet, instead of only returning objects that already exist. Second, the pass decorator factory takes an extra switch that turns on that behavior, so a decorated command runs on its own rather than stopping with the "Managed to invoke callback without a context object of type ... existing" error. Commands that do not turn the switch on keep the exact same behavior and the exact same error message as before, so nothing changes for anyone already relying on the old error.   25 │ Ease of use, with no change for existing programs.

  27 │ ## User experience
  28 │

   3 │ Complex Applications
   4 │ ====================
   5 │ 
   6 │ .. currentmodule:: click
   7 │ 
   8 │ Click is designed to write complex and simple CLI tools alike.  However
   9 │ the power of its design is the ability to arbitrarily nest systems

  11 │ realized that it provides a command line utility.  But so does Celery for

  13 │ to interact with each other and be cross configured.
  14 │ 
  15 │ In a theoretical world of two separate Click command line utilities they
  16 │ can solve this problem by nesting one inside the other.  For instance the
  17 │ web framework could also load the commands for the message queue
  18 │ framework.
  19 │ 
  20 │ Basic Concepts
  21 │ --------------
  22 │ 
  23 │ To understand how this works you need to understand two concepts: contexts
  24 │ and the calling convention.
  25 │ 
  26 │ Contexts
  27 │ ````````
  28 │ 
  29 │ Whenever a Click command is executed a :class:`Context` object is created
  30 │ which holds state for this particular invocation.  For instance it
  31 │ remembers parsed parameters, what command created it, which resources need
  32 │ to be cleaned up at the end of the function and so forth.  It also holds
  33 │ an application defined object optionally.
  34 │ 
  35 │ Context objects build a linked list until they hit top one.  Each context
  36 │ is linked to the parent context.  This allows a command to work below
  37 │ another command and store its own information there without having to be
  38 │ afraid of messing up the state of the parent command.
  39 │ 
  40 │ Because the parent data is however available it's possible to navigate to
  41 │ it if needed.
  42 │ 
  43 │ Most of the time you don't see the context object, but when writing more
  44 │ complex applications it comes in handy.  This brings us to the next point.
  45 │ 
  46 │ Calling Convention
  47 │ ``````````````````
  48 │ 
  49 │ When a Click command callback is executed it's passed all the non hidden
  50 │ parameters as keyword arguments.  Notably absent is the context.  However
  51 │ a callback can opt-into being passed the context object by marking itself
  52 │ with :func:`pass_context`.
  53 │ 
  54 │ So how do you invoke a command callback if you don't know if it should
  55 │ receive the context or not?  The answer is that the context itself
  56 │ provides a helper function (:meth:`Context.invoke`) which can do this for
  57 │ you.  It accepts the callback as first argument and then invokes the
  58 │ function correctly.
  59 │ 
  60 │ Building a Git
  61 │ --------------
  62 │ 
  63 │ In this example we want to build a command line tool that resembles a
  64 │ version control system a bit.  Systems like git usually provide one
  65 │ over-arching command that already accepts some parameters and
  66 │ configuration, and then has extra subcommands that do other things.
  67 │ 
  68 │ The Root Command
  69 │ ````````````````
  70 │ 
  71 │ At the top level we need a group that can hold all our commands.  In this
  72 │ case we use the basic :func:`click.group` which allows us to register
  73 │ other click commands below it.
  74 │ 
  75 │ For this command we also want to accept some parameters that configure the
  76 │ state of our tool:
  77 │ 
  78 │ .. click:example::
  79 │ 
  80 │     import os
  81 │     import click
  82 │ 
  83 │ 
  84 │     class Repo(object):
  85 │         def __init__(self, home, debug):
  86 │             self.home = os.path.abspath(home)
  87 │             self.debug = debug
  88 │ 
  89 │ 
  90 │     @click.group()
  91 │     @click.option('--repo-home', envvar='REPO_HOME', default='.repo')
  92 │     @click.option('--debug/--no-debug', default=False,
  93 │                   envvar='REPO_DEBUG')
  94 │     @click.pass_context
  95 │     def cli(ctx, repo_home, debug):
  96 │         ctx.obj = Repo(repo_home, debug)
  97 │ 
  98 │ 
  99 │ So let's understand what this does.  We create a group command which can
 100 │ have subcommands.  When it is invoked it will create an instance of a
 101 │ ``Repo`` class.  This holds the state for our command line tool.  In this
 102 │ case it just remembers some parameters but at this point it could also
 103 │ start loading config files and so on.
 104 │ 
 105 │ This state object is then remembered as :attr:`~Context.obj` on the
 106 │ context.  This is a special attribute where commands are supposed to
 107 │ remember what they need to pass on to their children.
 108 │ 
 109 │ In order for this to work we need to mark our function with
 110 │ :func:`pass_context` because otherwise the context object would be
 111 │ entirely hidden from us.
 112 │ 
 113 │ The First Child Command
 114 │ ```````````````````````
 115 │ 
 116 │ So let's add our first child command to it.  Let's go with the clone
 117 │ command:
 118 │ 
 119 │ .. click:example::
 120 │ 
 121 │     @cli.command()
 122 │     @click.argument('src')
 123 │     @click.argument('dest', required=False)
 124 │     def clone(src, dest):
 125 │         pass
 126 │ 
 127 │ So now we have a clone command, but how do we get access to the repo?  As
 128 │ you can imagine one way is to use the :func:`pass_context` function which
 129 │ again will make our callback also get the context passed on which we
 130 │ memorized the repo.  Even better there is a second version of this
 131 │ decorator called :func:`pass_obj` which will just pass the stored object,
 132 │ in our case the repo:
 133 │ 
 134 │ .. click:example::
 135 │ 
 136 │     @cli.command()
 137 │     @click.argument('src')
 138 │     @click.argument('dest', required=False)
 139 │     @click.pass_obj

 143 │ Interleaved Commands
 144 │ ````````````````````
 145 │ 
 146 │ While not relevant for this particular program we want to build there is
 147 │ also quite good support for interleaving systems.  Imagine for instance
 148 │ there would be this super cool plugin for our version control system that
 149 │ needs a lot of configuration and wants to store its own configuration as
 150 │ :attr:`~Context.obj`.  If we would then attach another command below that,
 151 │ all the sudden we would get the plugin config instead of our repo object.
 152 │ 
 153 │ One obvious way is to store a reference to the repo on the plugin but then
 154 │ a command needs to be aware that it's attached below such a plugin.
 155 │ 
 156 │ There is a much better system by taking advantage of the linked nature of
 157 │ contexts.  We know that the plugin context is linked to the context that

 159 │ level where the object stored on the context was a repo.

 163 │ case we know that we want to find the closest ``Repo`` object.  So let's

 165 │ 
 166 │ .. click:example::
 167 │ 
 168 │     pass_repo = click.make_pass_decorator(Repo)

 176 │     @click.argument('src')
 177 │     @click.argument('dest', required=False)
 178 │     @pass_repo
 179 │     def clone(repo, src, dest):
